 How VoteHub Spotted Republican Turnout Issues in Early Voting
 In this year's midterms, a strong early vote for Democrats translated to the party's turnout advantage in the election as a whole. VoteHub's analysis with L2 data was able to identify these trends well before Election Day. 
 November 19, 2026 
 by
 Zachary Donnini 
 Early voting was one of the strongest positive data points for Democrats this cycle. Throughout October, we spent time looking at who was turning out, who was not, and whether Republicans could count on the less frequent voters who had helped them in 2024 again in 2026. In state after state, the early voters with thin voting histories were much more Democratic than regular voters, indicating a big differential turnout advantage for Democrats.
 In the two months before Election Day, a lot of people are already voting, and we know who they are. Generally, in-person early voting (IPEV) is more useful for understanding turnout than mail returns (AB), as the fact that people have to leave their house to vote seems to be more predictive of final voter behavior. Early voting starts at different times in different states: Virginia’s 45-day IPEV period began in September, while the first high-information, heavy in-person early voting state Georgia began on October 13. As we have previously emphasized , the early vote tells us who is voting, not who they are voting for. It tells us how the electorate and turnout are shaping up, but does not measure persuasion. Nevertheless, this information is still very useful. Going from expecting a Florida electorate that favors Republicans by 12 points by registration to one that favors them by just nine, for example, suggests that the final results would be roughly three points bluer, assuming the same persuasion. But turnout data alone does not tell us very much, if anything, about persuasion, which introduces significant uncertainty about overall results, even with a good grasp on turnout.
 As early as September 25, Virginia’s initial early vote data had us warning that the downside for Republicans could be severe due to differential turnout; on October 14, we described a low enthusiasm election on the GOP side, and by October 21, North Carolina’s numbers were already historically bad for Republicans. Two days later we pointed to a specific problem in North Carolina and Georgia: that Republicans under the age 45 were showing little enthusiasm thus far. We were also flagging what this could mean for North Carolina’s House map, where the Republican gerrymander ended up collapsing. By October 29, it was clear that the gerrymander was at risk of breaking on the U.S. Senate level, leaving Republican House candidates needing to outrun Whatley to survive. That is what happened: Cooper carried all 14 districts in the state, and while some Republican House candidates outran Whatley by enough to survive, others did not. We are happy with how useful this analysis proved to be, and wanted to go through what we were seeing before Election Day.
 Most of this work came from joining L2 Data’s daily early vote files to voters’ histories. We are grateful for our partnership with L2 and for the excellent work they do. These files let us compare people who voted in 2024 with people who skipped it, primary voters with non-primary voters, and habitual early voters with people who usually waited until Election Day. We were looking at party registration in the twelve states that provided it, and used other information, including race and modeled vote, in states like Georgia and Texas.
 Voting history
 One of the most useful comparisons was between early voters who participated in the 2024 general election and those who did not, because it helped us assess whether the electorate was shaping up to be similar to, redder than, or bluer than 2024. By the end of early voting, voters turning out who did not in 2024 were more Democratic in all twelve registration states we tracked. 
 The partisanship gap among 2024 non-voters was 12.8 points in North Carolina, 13.6 in Kansas and 18.7 in Louisiana; in North Carolina, the gap grew from 6.7 points on October 19 to 9.9 on October 23 and 12.8 by the end of the early vote period. In the final weekdays in North Carolina, the people who had skipped 2024 were about 18 points more Democratic than the people who had voted in it.
 Florida was interesting because it started in the other direction during mail returns, which are often not very predictive of voting behavior. On October 19, early voters who participated in 2024 were slightly more Democratic than those who skipped it. That reversed as in-person voting began and continued, and by the end, the nonvoters were 5.1 points more Democratic. The daily gaps in the last week were around nine or ten points. 
 We got much the same answer using the last midterm. People who skipped 2022 were more Democratic than 2022 voters in eleven of the twelve states. The gap was 12.8 points in North Carolina, 10.2 in Florida and 16.8 in Louisiana.
 2026 primary voters
 We also compared early voters who participated in the 2026 primary with those who did not. We prefer this comparison because the vast majority of people who vote in 2026 will also have voted in 2024, so the more important group are people leaving the 2024 electorate, rather than joining it. We know from above that the people joining were very blue. Primary turnout gives us another way to estimate the composition of the broader electorate, including the much larger group that voted in 2024.
 A competitive Democratic or Republican primary can pull enough people to the polls to substantially change the primary electorate’s party split. If the general electorate is going to match a previous general election’s party split, the people who skipped a very blue primary, for example, would need to be much more Republican to balance out those who participated. So we use the full primary electorate’s party split and the gap between primary and non-primary voters to estimate how the non-primary voters will break down.
 The full 2026 primary electorate was 55.5% Democratic by two-way party registration in North Carolina, compared with 48.2% for the 2024 general electorate. Among people voting early in the general election, primary participants were 61.6% Democratic and non-primary participants were 57.4%. This means there was a positive primary gap of about four points, but the people who skipped the primary were still a very Democratic group. If that 4.2-point gap held through Election Day, applying it to the full primary electorate’s 55.5% Democratic share would imply a non-primary electorate that was about 51.3% Democratic. Both groups would still be bluer than the 2024 electorate’s 48.2%, and since primary voters generally make up about half of the general electorate, that would imply an overall Democratic share of 53.4% by two-way party registration. This still leaves two moving parts: modeling how the gap changes over time and estimating the attrition gap among primary voters. But both are simpler problems than estimating 2024 voter attrition from primary history alone, as above. We expected the electorate would be more blue than 53.4% Democratic, since there would be more attrition among Republican primary voters than Democratic primary voters, and we believed for a variety of reasons that the gap would likely shrink on Election Day, but this data allowed us to establish the rough heuristic that the electorate would be substantially to the left of 2024, even moreso than other states.
 Florida had a different starting point: its full primary electorate was 42.9% Democratic, compared with 41.9% in the 2024 general electorate. Among early voters, those who participated in the primary were 48.1% Democratic, while those who skipped it were 49.1%. That negative primary gap was encouraging for Democrats because non-primary voters were bluer than primary voters, and this is why we knew going into Election Day that the 2026 electorate would be bluer than the 2024 electorate (even with very red domestic migration patterns). It ended up favoring Republicans by 12 in 2026, compared with by 16 in 2024, by two-way party registration.
 The key reason we use this method, and consider it stronger than looking at 2024 or using turnout stratified by propensity in the last three elections, is that in the historical data we’ve examined, primary voters consistently turn out in the general election at rates above 95% for both parties, and the partisan turnout gap had always been less than two percentage points. This means primary voter attrition gaps are much easier to estimate than 3/3 or 2/3 attrition gaps based on voting history, and even a poor estimate won’t change the final result very much. Given how weak Republican turnout was this year, the gap may well have exceeded 2% in some states in 2026. In Georgia, the only state we have data for so far, it was 0.7% (96.6% – 95.9%). However, the full primary electorate is still a useful starting point, since we can assume the lion’s share of those voters will turn out on both sides. With their party composition close to known, we can use the early-voting gap between primary and non-primary voters to help estimate the composition of people who skipped the primary.
 This data explains the rapid late increase in expectations for Cooper and North Carolina’s Democratic House candidates, as well as Democrats across the country. For example, the data in Louisiana was also historically bad for Republicans, with a nearly evenly split primary electorate and only a small gap among early voters, compared with a much more Republican electorate in 2024. 1 
 Habitual early voters
 Of course, Republicans could still vote on Election Day; however, the above methods built on propensity analysis made it clear that Republicans would not just catch up entirely. Although one could argue that low-propensity Republicans were disproportionately more likely to vote on Election Day compared to low-propensity Democrats than high-propensity Republicans were compared to high-propensity Democrats, there is no strong precedent for this and we should not be surprised this did not happen again this year. This is more possible in a Northern state with more of the vote cast on Election Day; however, there is only so much Election Day voting can do in a state like North Carolina, where it makes up a small share of the vote.
 Realistically, the best case for Republicans was that although they still did poorly turning out their low-propensity voters, they would at least have a decent showing among their mid- and high-propensity voters. To test whether Republicans were simply waiting, another useful comparison was their past voting history by method. North Carolina let us do that, as we compared voters with similar histories going into 2022 and 2026. By October 30, Democrats were ahead of the final 2022 early turnout rate in all four groups while Republicans were behind.
 We ran another version at the end of early voting using the previous three generals: among people who voted early in all three, 85.1% of Democrats had voted, compared with 72.6% of Republicans. The equivalent groups in 2022 had finished at 76.0% and 74.1%. The 12.5% partisan gap here was larger than anything we could find in backtesting. This made it clear that North Carolina was heading toward a substantial partisan turnout gap among three-of-three voters, which could produce an unusually large overall turnout differential that we ended up getting. That fit with what we were seeing elsewhere: with a nearly unprecedented gap among low- and mid-propensity voters, we would expect at least some meaningful gap among high-propensity voters as well. 
 The final early vote numbers were extraordinary: Republicans did not win a single day of early voting. Even as more high-propensity Republicans joined the electorate in the last days of early voting, Democratic strength among less frequent voters still allowed them to win the final days. In the end, Cooper won by 19 points and carried all 14 congressional districts, helping break the gerrymander in the U.S. House level as Democrats won eight seats that Trump won by double-digits in 2024.
 Race
 Georgia does not have party registration, but the lions’ share of votes are cast before Election Day, so we looked closely at race and voting history. The Black share began very strong, but we expected that share to fall as more white voters turned out. The question was how far it would fall, and whether irregular Black voters would keep showing up. By the end of early voting, Black voters made up 35.3% of ballots, while on the comparable Friday before Election Day, the Black share was 33.5% in 2022 and 29.7% in 2024.
 But comparing Black early vote share from year to year directly has limited utility because voting patterns change from year to year. What really matters is the voting history breakdown: from October 16 to October 27, the share of Black early ballots coming from people who voted in no more than two of the previous three general elections rose from 18.2% to 24.9%. The corresponding white share rose from 15.6% to 19.2%. Given that this 5.7% gap has a historical tendency to grow on Election Day, this was also highly concerning for Republicans. Also concerning for Republicans was that low-propensity white early voters outside metropolitan Atlanta were far behind low-propensity white early voters from within, and the comparison between primary and non-primary voter analysis aligned with the general propensity analysis. This suggested that the early vote in Georgia was also suboptimal for the Republican Party; in retrospect, it was probably only marginally better than in North Carolina, and Ossoff won the Senate race by a large margin, with Keisha Lance Bottoms winning easily as well.
 Age
 The early electorate was still old, as expected in a midterm. However, the younger voters who did show up were substantially more Democratic than in 2024. We could see this especially clearly in Florida and North Carolina. The issue for Republicans was that this was not just about 18–29-year-olds, who make up a very small share of the electorate; rather, it was also true of the larger group of 30–44 voters, and the problem was almost just as bad there. Eight days before Election Day, Florida’s early voters aged 18–44 had a two-party registration margin of D+35.9, compared with R+7.0 at the same point in 2024. That is a 42.9-point swing, compared with 12.9 points among voters 45 and older. In North Carolina, the corresponding shifts were 54.6 points among younger voters and 22.9 points among older voters.
 The gap actually grew as Republicans started having better days overall as older, high-propensity Republicans were finally voting, but younger Republicans remained largely absent. We kept seeing the same pattern across these comparisons, which gave us more confidence in what they were telling us. Democratic voters who skipped recent elections were reasonably activated, while Republicans were relying much more heavily on their regular voters.
 While the 2024 vs. non-2024 gap or the 2026 primary vs. nonprimary gap methods are easier to communicate, internally we divided early voters into four nonoverlapping groups: those who voted in the 2026 primary; those who voted in 2022 but skipped the 2026 primary; those who voted in 2024 but neither of those elections; and those who voted in none of the three. We then applied each of the three groups’ gaps relative to primary voters to the primary group’s expected final composition, which we know to within a percentage point or so. Weighting these estimates by each group’s expected share of the electorate in each state gives us a strong picture of the final electorate. We think this approach gives us the richest and most informative data to work with, although the 2026 primary vs. nonprimary gap alone gets you a lot of the way there. ↩︎
